items.title: Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2022
items.q: The other thing just in general is that the pianist in our group, Chuck Lamb, and a guitarist, Mike DeMicco and Dan and I, it’s a highly democratic process you know.

ctx.x: I think you know certain things, I’ll hear other ways to play something like for instance in “Kathy’s Waltz,” I’ve always heard that that could be a great kind of reggae-feeling thing, which you wouldn’t think of right away but we tried it and it was like hey that actually works great. And I remember at the recording session Mike had worked out this whole opening thing and it was like, “Oh yeah, that works great but I’d really like to play a chordal guitar thing.” And it was like, “Well do that in the beginning…

The other thing just in general is that the pianist in our group, Chuck Lamb, and a guitarist, Mike DeMicco and Dan and I, it’s a highly democratic process you know. So when we put out a record or when we do a concert, it is sort of like a Venn diagram of all the things that we happen to think is cool, probably much to our commercial demise you know, well in terms of like for example none of us wants to make a record that sounds anything like any Kenny G record. Sorry, Kenny. Or any of the hundreds of sax players…

for “Kathy’s Waltz” it’s just interesting to think of when “Kathy’s Waltz” was written reggae didn’t even exist. You know? So because our dad went out to the Middle East and he incorporated music that didn’t exist in the United States like the Turkish beat that became “Blue Rondo” I feel like he sort of gave us the grand rights to explore and put other music into our re-interpretations of his music. If he were our age he’d be doing it. And the other thing is because of our age we all have a rock & roll kind of…
